title: The fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:14–17)
hookLine: believers are like a sweet smell spreading, and it lands two ways
tomorrow: who needs a reference letter when people can read your life?

lines: DEATH UNTO DEATH, LIFE UNTO LIFE.
cards: Bleach in a hallway. To one person it says clean, safe, someone's taking care of this. To another it says hospital, bad news, wait here.

Same smell, two opposite messages. Paul writes a line like that, and it's odd: "To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life." One scent, two verdicts.
How does that work, and why is he thanking God for it?

teach.h: NO REST AT TROAS, THEN THANKS.
teach.b: Back up a few verses. Paul's plans have just fallen apart. At Troas a door was open to preach, and still he had no rest, because his friend Titus wasn't there, so he left.

The very next line is thanks: "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place." Savour is the King James word for a scent.
Some readers hear a Roman victory parade in that word triumph, with incense burning along the route.
Then Paul makes the people the scent: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish." That's the puzzle solved. The scent doesn't change.
The people breathing it in do. Paul doesn't control how it lands; he only carries it. Which is why he asks, "And who is sufficient for these things?"
He leaves that question hanging. He only says what he won't do: he won't water the message down to sell it.
He'll speak "as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God."
One to tell a friend tonight: a smile can be faked for a while, but a scent is either on you or it isn't.

how: In churches that use incense, its scent rising is linked with prayer; some Christians recall 2 Corinthians 2:15 as a call to carry something of Christ into ordinary places.

games.q: what does “the fragrance of christ” mean?
o: a perfume worn to church on feast days
the smell of incense after a long service
a scent of Christ carried into every place

games.q: the fragrance of Christ — tap the pairs.
p: a door open, and no rest
the King James word for a scent

s: Paul says believers smell sweet only to people who already agree
the same savour lands as life to some and as death to others.
Paul gives thanks right after his plans at Troas fell apart
no rest in his spirit, he left, and the next line is now thanks be unto God.
Paul answers 'who is sufficient for these things?' right away
he leaves it hanging here; he only says he'll speak as of sincerity.

games.q: you're known at school as the one who prays before lunch. some people find it kind; others find it weird. what fits Paul's picture?
o: keep it sincere; one scent lands two ways, and you only carry it.
stop; anything that bothers someone must be done the wrong way.
pray louder, so the ones who think it's weird hear it more.
games.why: to the one we are the savour of death unto death; to the other the savour of life unto life. Paul doesn't control how it lands. he carries it, as of sincerity.

practice: Smell something close by: your sleeve, a cup of coffee, the soap on your hands, the air by a window. Notice how a scent arrives before a word is said, and stays after you've gone.
Then think of one room you'll walk into today, and what you'd want to linger there when you leave.

wordCard.voice: The fragrance of Christ. Paul's picture of believers as a scent carried into every place, received in more than one way.

orig.note: Greek: a sweet smell, fragrance; the 'sweet savour' of 2 Corinthians 2:15.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: a sweet savor, carried with sincerity into every room and never faked. Go gently.
